One neighborhood, layer by layer

Start with a neighborhood that was redlined in 1937, such as Pleasant Hill in Macon. Then press a button to drop a layer onto the same map: internet access, crime, education, or food deserts. Each layer can be viewed alone or stacked on the others.

Where the numbers come from

  • Redlining: 1937–1940 Home Owners' Loan Corporation maps (Mapping Inequality).
  • Internet access: U.S. Census ACS 2020–2024, table B28002, for the Census block groups that overlap each 1937 area. Each figure covers whole block groups, which can extend past the 1937 boundary, so it is not a rate for the redlined land alone. A block group touching two grades counts in both. Each neighborhood is compared with the average across the city's 1937-mapped areas, which is not a citywide figure (the published Census figure for Macon-Bibb County as a whole is 89.6%): within 3 points counts as about average, and more than 8 points is the darkest shade.
  • Crime: for Birmingham, Mobile, Montgomery, New Orleans, Seattle and Tacoma the page shows averages by 1937 grade from the project's 209-precinct study in eight cities, looked up one precinct at a time (Grade A: 4,563; Grade B: 4,918; Grade C: 5,584; Grade D: 6,204 per 100,000). They are not rates for single neighborhoods, and the underlying precinct records, years and population counts are still being checked, so treat them as provisional. For Macon, the layer uses the sheriff's incident records that Macon-Bibb County publishes on its map server (layer “Crime_Jan_to_Jun_2019”): all 4,450 records, reported 1 January–30 June 2019, ten offense types. Each record is counted in the 1937 area its map point falls in; the page shows counts only, never addresses or case numbers. 7 records whose map points fall outside the county are left out. 97.7% of records carry the same precinct code as the official sheriff's precinct boundaries (Macon-Bibb County open data, 2018). Shading is offenses per square mile of the 1937 area, not a rate per resident, because no population count exists for the 1937 boundaries; shopping centers and busy roads raise counts where they sit. Areas with fewer than 5 offenses are not shaded. The layer has not yet been confirmed with the sheriff's Crime Analysis Unit. The 2014 county figure from the Urban Redevelopment Plan (10,279 incidents, 6,674 inside the redevelopment area) remains the latest published annual total.
  • Education: for Macon, Georgia Milestones End-of-Grade results for 2024–25 from the Governor's Office of Student Achievement: the share of all tested students scoring proficient or distinguished, compared with the Bibb County district figure for grades 3–8 (math 21.7%, English language arts 22.7%). Four schools are mapped so far; Springdale Elementary (math 48.6%) lies north of the map. For the other cities, the project's 92-school data set (Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, Washington), compared with the average of the study schools on that city's map. A school inside an area is not necessarily the school its residents attend.
  • Food deserts: USDA Economic Research Service, Food Access Research Atlas, 2019 (2010 census tracts). A hatched tract is low-income and has a large share of residents more than 1 mile from a supermarket (10 miles in rural tracts). Tracts are drawn on current boundaries; tracts whose boundaries changed after 2010 and cannot be matched are left blank. Tracts are larger than 1937 areas, so each neighborhood reports the tracts that its block groups fall in. For Macon the layer also marks 5 public libraries and 3 hospitals (addresses from the library system's and the hospitals' own web pages, checked September 2026) and gives the straight-line distance from the middle of each area to the nearest one; it is not a travel distance, and other necessities such as pharmacies are not mapped yet.
  • Street detail: for Macon, local streets and street names from U.S. Census TIGER/Line appear as you zoom in. The ⌖ button zooms to the selected neighborhood.
  • Side by side: the default pair is illustrative: one Grade D area and one Grade A (or B) area from the same 1937 map, chosen for the demonstration. It becomes a research comparison only once the rule for choosing a comparable neighborhood is written down before outcomes are compared. Any two areas can be chosen from the lists.
  • The atlas lets you examine whether these measures differ across historically graded areas. Any difference is an association; it does not by itself show that the 1937 grades caused it.
